headline: Healey's first Budget scraps gas standing charges and doubles the bank surcharge to 6%

terms.meaning: A fixed daily fee on an energy bill, paid whatever you use.
An extra tax on banks' profits, on top of normal corporation tax.
The return investors get on UK government bonds; it shows the cost of government borrowing.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget scraps gas standing charges and doubles the bank surcharge to 6%
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October, abolishing standing charges on gas bills for around 23 million homes and raising the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.
The government says the surcharge will raise £1.5 billion to help fund household and business support. The Budget speech also promised a £100 winter payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends.
The Office for Budget Responsibility upgraded its growth forecast to 1.2% this year, then 1% next year. But debt interest costs are £14 billion higher this year, and headroom against the government's fiscal rules is £9 billion lower than in March.
The yield on the 10-year gilt fell about 2 basis points to 5.323% as Healey spoke, a broadly positive market reaction.
levels.why: It shows how the government is paying for energy support while borrowing costs stay high.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget removes gas standing charges and raises the bank surcharge
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget on 28 October to scrap standing charges on gas bills, which affects around 23 million homes, and to double the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027.
Ministers say the surcharge will bring in £1.5 billion towards support for households and businesses, including a £100 winter payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Healey promised no tax rises on wages or dividends.
The official forecaster, the OBR, now expects growth of 1.2% this year and 1% next year. Yet higher interest on government debt, up £14 billion this year, has cut the room for manoeuvre by £9 billion compared with March.
Government bond yields dipped slightly as the Chancellor spoke, suggesting investors were broadly comfortable.
levels.why: The Budget tries to ease winter bills without raising taxes on workers, but the public finances remain tight.

levels.headline: Budget cuts energy costs for homes and taxes banks more
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, set out his first Budget on 28 October. It removes standing charges, the fixed daily fees on gas bills, for around 23 million homes. The cost is partly covered by a bigger tax on banks.
The bank surcharge goes from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027, raising an expected £1.5 billion. There will also be a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Healey said wages and dividends will not face higher taxes. The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year. However, the government is spending £14 billion more on debt interest, which leaves less spare money for future plans.
Bond markets reacted calmly, with borrowing costs edging down.
levels.why: Many households will see lower fixed energy costs, while banks face a bigger tax bill.

levels.headline: Chancellor scraps gas standing charges and taxes banks more in first Budget
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey has delivered his first Budget, promising help with energy bills and paying for part of it by taxing banks more.
Standing charges, the fixed daily amount on a gas bill, will go for around 23 million homes. Instead, those costs will be added to the price of each unit of gas used. The bank surcharge will double from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027 and is expected to raise £1.5 billion. A £100 winter payment is planned for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. The official forecast for growth this year is 1.2%. But the government now pays £14 billion more in debt interest, so it has less room to spend.
levels.why: It affects what families pay to heat their homes this winter.

levels.headline: Budget: gas standing charges to go, banks to pay more tax
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey has announced his first Budget. The main aim is to help families with energy bills this winter.
A standing charge is a fixed fee you pay each day for a gas supply, even if you use none. The Budget removes it for around 23 million homes, and the cost moves into the price of the gas itself. There will also be a £100 payment for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
To help pay, banks will pay a higher extra tax on their profits. It rises from 3% to 6% for 15 months from January 2027 and should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said he would not raise taxes on wages or dividends.
The government is also paying £14 billion more in interest on its debts this year, which limits what it can spend.
levels.why: It could lower fixed costs on household energy bills, but the government still has little spare money.

levels.headline: Budget helps with energy bills and makes banks pay more
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, has set out the government's plans for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget.
Gas bills have a fixed daily fee called a standing charge. You pay it even if you use no gas. The Budget ends this fee for around 23 million homes. The cost will be added to the price of the gas people use instead. There will also be a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits for a while. The extra tax goes from 3% to 6% and should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said workers will not pay higher taxes on wages.
The government also owes a lot of money and must pay interest on it, now £14 billion more than before.
levels.why: It changes how some household bills are charged and who pays for the help.

levels.headline: The Budget: help with gas bills, and a bigger tax for banks
levels.body:
Every year the Chancellor says how the government will raise and spend money. This year the Chancellor is John Healey, and he spoke on 28 October.
One big change is to gas bills. Most bills include a fixed daily fee, called a standing charge, which you pay even if you use no gas. It is going for around 23 million homes. Another is a £100 payment this winter for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. Council tax bands sort homes by value.
The money comes partly from banks. They will pay a bigger extra tax, 6% instead of 3%, for 15 months. That should raise £1.5 billion. Healey said taxes on wages will not go up.
The government borrows money too, and the interest it pays has risen by £14 billion this year.
levels.why: It affects the bills families pay to keep warm.

levels.headline: A big plan for money: help with heating bills
levels.body:
Once a year, the person in charge of the government's money explains the plan. This person is the Chancellor. This year it is John Healey.
He said gas bills will change. At the moment many bills have a fixed fee each day, even if you use no gas. That fee is called a standing charge. It will end for around 23 million homes. Some families will also get £100 this winter to help with heating.
Where does the money come from? Banks will pay more tax. A tax is money people and firms pay to the government. Banks will pay twice as much extra tax for a while, 6% instead of 3%. That should raise £1.5 billion.
The government also owes money and pays interest on it. That bill has grown by £14 billion.
levels.why: It could make heating a home cheaper for many families this winter.

levels.headline: The government has a plan to help with heating bills
levels.body:
The Chancellor looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. He has made a plan for the year.
Many homes pay a fixed fee for gas each day. It does not matter how much gas they use. This fee will stop. Around 23 million homes will not pay it. Some families will also get £100 this winter to help pay for heat.
The government needs money to pay for this. It will ask banks to pay more tax. Tax is money that firms and people give to the government. Banks will pay a bit more for just over a year. That will raise £1.5 billion.
The government also borrowed money before. It has to pay a fee called interest for borrowing. That fee is now bigger.
levels.why: It may help families keep their homes warm.

levels.headline: Helping families stay warm
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a money jar. A grown-up called the Chancellor decides how it is used. His name is John Healey.
He said families should pay less for heating. Some bills have a daily fee, like paying to enter a shop before you buy anything. That fee will stop for gas in around 23 million homes. Some families will also get £100 this winter.
To fill the jar, banks will pay more tax. Tax is money shared to pay for things everyone uses. The banks will pay a bit more for just over a year, and that should bring in £1.5 billion.
The country has also borrowed money, a bit like borrowing pocket money. It must pay a little extra for that, and the extra has grown.
levels.why: It is meant to help families keep warm without the government spending money it has not got.

headline: Wall Street falls as Alphabet suffers its worst day ever, ending the S&P 500's three-day rise

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
The cash a company has left after paying its running costs and investments.
An index dominated by technology companies.

levels.headline: Wall Street falls as Alphabet suffers its worst day ever, ending the S&P 500's three-day rise
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed down about 0.3% at 7,720.39 on Thursday 29 October, the last completed session, ending a three-day winning run. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 132.54 points, or 0.25%, to 52,342.56, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.38% to 26,184.72.
The main drag was Alphabet, the owner of Google. Its shares fell nearly 13% in their worst day since it listed in 2004, wiping out roughly $500 billion in market value. The company missed forecasts for revenue and earnings in the third quarter and reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion.
Alphabet kept its 2026 capital spending forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion. Renewed doubts about how long the heavy spending on artificial intelligence can pay off weighed on other technology shares.
levels.why: A single giant company's results can move the whole market and the savings and pensions tied to it.

levels.headline: US stocks slip as Alphabet tumbles on a disappointing quarter
levels.body:
US shares ended lower on Thursday 29 October, the latest completed session. The S&P 500 fell about 0.3% to close at 7,720.39, its first fall after three straight gains. The Dow lost 132.54 points, or 0.25%, to 52,342.56, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.38% to 26,184.72.
Alphabet, Google's parent company, led the decline. It fell almost 13%, its biggest one-day drop since going public in 2004, after missing expectations for revenue and profit and reporting negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion.
Investors are uneasy about how much big technology firms are spending on artificial intelligence. Alphabet said it still expects to spend $195 billion to $205 billion this year, and that unease spread to other tech stocks.
levels.why: It shows how much the market now depends on the AI spending plans of a few large firms.

levels.headline: US shares fall after Alphabet's weak results
levels.body:
The main US stock index, the S&P 500, closed down about 0.3% on Thursday 29 October, finishing at 7,720.39. That was the last full trading session. It ended three days of gains.
The Dow Jones fell 132.54 points, or 0.25%, to 52,342.56. The Nasdaq, which holds many technology firms, dropped 1.38% to 26,184.72.
The fall was driven by Alphabet, the company behind Google. Its shares dropped almost 13%, the biggest one-day fall since it joined the stock market in 2004. It had missed forecasts for sales and profit. It also spent more cash than it brought in, with negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion.
Some investors now worry that the huge sums spent on artificial intelligence may not pay off quickly.
levels.why: Falls in big technology shares can affect pension funds and savings that hold them.

levels.headline: Wall Street ends lower as Google's owner has its worst day

levels.headline: US shares fall because Google's owner had a bad quarter

Share prices in the United States went down on Thursday 29 October. This was the last full day of trading. A stock index is a score showing how a group of shares is doing. The S&P 500 covers 500 big firms. It fell about 0.3% to 7,720.39 after three days of rising.

levels.headline: Share prices fall after a big company's bad news
levels.body:
A share is a tiny slice of a company. When many people want it, its price goes up. When they do not, it goes down.
On Thursday 29 October, the main score for American shares, the S&P 500, went down by about 0.3%. Two other scores, the Dow and the Nasdaq, went down by 0.25% and 1.38%.

levels.headline: Why share prices went down

Think of a school sale where everyone swaps cards. If a very popular card suddenly looks less special, many children want it less. Its price drops. Shares work in a similar way.
On Thursday 29 October, share prices in America went down. The main score, the S&P 500, fell a little, about 0.3%. A score called the Nasdaq fell more, by 1.38%.

levels.headline: Why some shares got cheaper

Imagine a toy that everyone wants. Then people hear it is not as good as they thought. Fewer people want it, so it gets cheaper. That happened to some shares in America on Thursday.

headline: Burnham offers devolved governments a partnership on regional empowerment at the first National Economic Council for the nations

terms.meaning: Moving decision-making powers from central government to nations, regions or cities.
The governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, which control some of their own affairs.
Rebuilding manufacturing and other industry in places that lost it.

levels.headline: Burnham offers devolved governments a partnership on regional empowerment at the first National Economic Council for the nations
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales, John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth, in Glasgow on 30 October for the first National Economic Council for the nations. Northern Ireland was also represented. It is the first such meeting since he became Prime Minister.
According to a GOV.UK release, Burnham used the meeting to offer each devolved government a partnership on regional empowerment, telling them to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK". The agenda covered opportunities for young people, reindustrialisation and giving regions and cities more decision-making power.
He is pitching devolution that goes deeper within nations, rather than only moving powers between parliaments. The release also said £1 billion will be invested across the UK over four years in innovation clusters. No concrete decisions from the talks had been published at the time of writing.
levels.why: It shows how the new Prime Minister wants to share power between Westminster, the nations and local areas.

levels.headline: Burnham meets First Ministers in Glasgow and offers a partnership on devolution
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Scotland's First Minister John Swinney and Wales's First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth on 30 October in Glasgow for the first National Economic Council for the nations. Northern Ireland was represented too.
A government release said Burnham offered each devolved government a partnership, urging them to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK". Talks were due to cover young people's opportunities, rebuilding industry and handing more decisions to regions and cities.
He argues for devolution within the nations, not just between parliaments. The government also pointed to £1 billion of investment over four years in innovation clusters, groups of research and business hubs. The outcome of the talks had not been published.
levels.why: The meeting tests whether the UK government and the devolved governments can agree on shared economic goals.

levels.headline: PM invites Scotland and Wales to work together on regional power
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, met the leaders of Scotland and Wales, John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth, in Glasgow on 30 October. It was the first meeting of a new body called the National Economic Council for the nations. Northern Ireland also took part.
The government says Burnham offered each devolved government a partnership and asked them to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK". Topics included jobs for young people, rebuilding industry and giving regions and cities more say in decisions.
The government also highlighted £1 billion of investment over four years in innovation clusters across the UK. There was no word yet on any firm decisions.
levels.why: It could change how much power towns, cities and nations have over their own economies.

levels.headline: Prime Minister meets Scotland and Wales leaders to talk about sharing power
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham met the First Ministers of Scotland and Wales, John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth, in Glasgow on 30 October. The meeting was the first National Economic Council for the nations, and Northern Ireland was represented as well.
The government says Burnham offered each of them a partnership. He asked them to "work with me to empower every single part of the UK". They were due to discuss jobs and chances for young people, bringing industry back to places that lost it, and giving regions and cities more say.
The government also said £1 billion will be invested over four years in innovation clusters, which are areas where new ideas and businesses grow together. No decisions had been announced.
levels.why: It affects who makes decisions about jobs and money where people live.

levels.headline: PM meets leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. On 30 October he met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow. They are John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth. Northern Ireland was there too.

levels.why: It is about who decides things in your area, such as jobs and training.

levels.headline: PM meets Scotland and Wales leaders to talk about sharing power more widely

levels.headline: The Prime Minister meets Scotland and Wales to share power

Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. On 30 October he met two leaders in Glasgow, John Swinney of Scotland and Rhun ap Iorwerth of Wales. Northern Ireland sent people as well.

levels.why: It could mean more local control over things that affect young people's futures.

levels.headline: Leaders meet to talk about sharing power across the UK
levels.body:
The Prime Minister is called Andy Burnham. On 30 October he met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in a city called Glasgow. Their names are John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth.
The UK is made of four parts: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Some parts have their own governments to make some choices. Burnham asked them to work together. He wants more choices to be made close to where people live, in towns and cities too.
They talked about jobs for young people and building things again in places that used to make lots of goods. The government also said it will spend £1 billion over four years to help new ideas grow. Nothing has been decided yet.
levels.why: Choices made nearby can shape jobs and schools for young people.

levels.headline: Leaders talk about sharing the job of running the country
levels.body:
The UK has four parts: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The leader of the whole country is the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham. On 30 October he met the leaders of Scotland and Wales in Glasgow.
Some of the parts make their own choices on things like schools. Burnham asked them to work with him. He wants towns and cities to have a say too, not just the big governments.
They talked about jobs for young people and about making things in factories again. The government also said it will spend £1 billion over four years to help new ideas grow into businesses. Nobody has said yet what will be decided.
levels.why: Where decisions are made can change what happens in your own town.

levels.headline: Grown-ups meet to share the work
levels.body:
Think of a school with a head teacher and different class teachers. The head makes some choices. The class teachers make others. The UK is a bit like that.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, is like the head. On 30 October he met the leaders of Scotland and Wales, John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth. They run their own parts of the UK for some things.
Burnham asked them to work together as a team. He would like even more choices to be made in towns and cities. They talked about jobs for young people. The government also said it will spend £1 billion to help new ideas grow. Nobody has said what will be decided yet.
levels.why: Good teamwork between leaders can help young people find work later.

headline: Burnham wants an 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of the 20 November Brussels summit

terms.meaning: The right of people in EU countries to live and work in each other's countries without a visa.
A plan letting young people live and work abroad for a limited time.
The EU trading area with shared rules on goods, services and people.

levels.headline: Burnham wants an 'honest discussion' on EU free movement ahead of the 20 November Brussels summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK should have an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit, as the UK and EU prepare for a summit in Brussels on 20 November, according to Euronews reporting of a Sunday Times interview.
He has ruled out joining the euro or the Schengen travel area, and has said he is committed to the 2024 Labour manifesto, which ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union. No agreement on free movement has been confirmed.
On the table at the summit are a trade deal on food and drink, progress on linking emissions trading and energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. The sides are far apart on youth visas: the UK has pushed for a cap below 50,000, Brussels up to 150,000. Nigel Farage called Burnham's comments a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: The summit could set the UK's relationship with its biggest trading partner for years.

levels.headline: Burnham calls for 'honest discussion' on free movement before UK-EU summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called for an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit, ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November. The comments came in a Sunday Times interview reported by Euronews.
Burnham has ruled out joining the euro or Schengen and says he stands by the 2024 Labour manifesto, which ruled out free movement, single market membership and a customs union. Nothing on free movement has been agreed.
The summit agenda includes a food and drink trade deal, linking emissions trading and energy systems, a youth experience scheme and cooperation on immigration. The UK wants fewer than 50,000 young visas, while the EU wants up to 150,000. Nigel Farage described Burnham's remarks as a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: How far the UK moves towards the EU is a major political and economic question.

levels.headline: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on free movement as EU summit nears
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the UK should have an "honest discussion" about immigration since Brexit. He spoke before a summit between the UK and the EU in Brussels on 20 November, in an interview with the Sunday Times reported by Euronews.
He has ruled out joining the euro or the Schengen travel area. He says he is bound by the 2024 Labour manifesto, which rejected free movement, the single market and a customs union. No deal on free movement has been confirmed.

The two sides disagree on visa numbers for young people, with the UK suggesting under 50,000 and the EU up to 150,000. Nigel Farage said the comments were a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: It is a test of how close the UK will get to the EU after Brexit.

levels.headline: PM wants 'honest discussion' about free movement before EU summit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Britain should have an "honest discussion" about how immigration has changed since Brexit. A UK-EU summit will be held in Brussels on 20 November.
Free movement means people from EU countries can live and work in each other's countries without a visa. Burnham has not agreed to bring it back. He has ruled out joining the euro or the Schengen travel zone, and says he stands by Labour's 2024 manifesto, which ruled out free movement, the single market and a customs union.
The summit will look at food and drink trade, energy links, a youth experience scheme and immigration. The UK has suggested fewer than 50,000 visas for young people, while the EU wants up to 150,000. Nigel Farage called the comments a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: The talks could change trade, travel and work rules for Britons and Europeans.

levels.headline: PM says UK should talk honestly about free movement with the EU
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, says the UK should have an "honest discussion" about immigration since Brexit. A big meeting between the UK and the EU is due in Brussels on 20 November.
Free movement is a rule that lets people from EU countries live and work in each other's countries without needing a visa. The UK left it when it left the EU in 2020. Burnham has not agreed to bring it back. He has said no to the euro and to the Schengen travel area. He also says he will stick to Labour's 2024 promises, which ruled out free movement.
At the summit they will talk about trade in food and drink, energy, and a scheme for young people to live and work abroad. They disagree on how many young people should be allowed. Nigel Farage called the comments a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: It could affect trade and whether young people can live and work abroad.

levels.headline: Burnham says the UK should talk plainly about free movement before the EU summit

levels.headline: PM open to talks about free movement before a UK and EU meeting
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says Britain should have an "honest discussion" about how many people have come to the UK since Brexit. Brexit is when the UK left the EU. The UK and the EU will meet in Brussels on 20 November.
Free movement means people in EU countries can live and work in each other's countries without a visa. Burnham has not said it will come back. He has said the UK will not join the euro or the Schengen travel area. He also says Labour promised in 2024 not to bring back free movement.
They will talk about food trade, energy, and a scheme for young people to live and work abroad for a time. The two sides disagree on how many young people can take part. Nigel Farage said the comments were a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
levels.why: The meeting could decide how easy it is to trade with and travel to Europe.

levels.headline: PM wants to talk openly about free movement with Europe
levels.body:
Brexit was when the UK left the European Union, the group of countries in Europe that work closely together. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, now says the UK should have an "honest discussion" about people moving between the UK and the EU. A big meeting is planned in Brussels on 20 November.
Free movement means people from EU countries can live and work in each other's countries without a visa. Burnham has not said it will come back. He says he will keep Labour's 2024 promise, which was not to bring it back.
At the meeting they will talk about trading food and drink and a plan for young people to live and work abroad for a while. The two sides disagree about how many young people can go. Nigel Farage was angry about the comments.
levels.why: It could change how easy it is for young people to study or work abroad.

levels.headline: The UK and Europe plan to talk
levels.body:
The UK used to be part of the European Union, a group of countries that work together. The UK left in 2020. This is called Brexit. Now the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, wants an honest talk about how people move between the UK and Europe.
There will be a big meeting in Brussels on 20 November. They will talk about selling food and drink, about energy, and about a plan for young people to live and work abroad for a short time. The two sides do not agree yet on how many young people can take part.
Burnham has not said people will be free to move again. Some politicians, such as Nigel Farage, were very unhappy about his words.
levels.why: It might change how young people can study or work in other countries.

levels.headline: Britain and its neighbours plan a big chat
levels.body:
Imagine you used to be in a big club with your neighbours. Then you left. Now you are talking about how you might work together again. That is a bit like Britain and the European Union.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, says he wants an honest chat about people moving between the UK and Europe. There will be a big meeting on 20 November in a city called Brussels.
They will talk about swapping food and drink, sharing energy, and letting young people live and work in another country for a short time. They do not yet agree on how many young people can go. Some people were angry about the chat. Nothing has been decided yet.
levels.why: It might one day change where young people can go to work or study.

headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% as markets expect the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 November

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
Inflation leaving out food and energy, which swing a lot.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage and savings rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation jumps to 3.5% as markets expect the Bank of England to raise rates on 5 November
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists expected. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%.
Fuel was the main driver, with motor fuel prices up 29.8% on a year earlier. Services inflation has also quickened, which analysts read as a sign that higher energy costs are feeding through to the wider economy.
The Bank of England's benchmark Bank Rate is 3.75%, against a 2% inflation target. Markets strongly expect a rise at the next meeting on 5 November, which would be the first since 2023, and one note said traders had priced in at least three quarter-point rises by April 2027.
The Budget forecasts say inflation will peak at 3.8% in early 2027.
levels.why: Higher rates would raise borrowing costs for mortgage holders and businesses.

levels.headline: Inflation rises to 3.5% and a Bank of England rate rise looks likely next week
levels.body:
UK inflation climbed to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, beating forecasts of 3.4%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, rose to 2.8% from 2.6%.
Motor fuel prices were 29.8% higher than a year earlier and were the biggest cause. Services inflation also picked up, suggesting higher energy costs are spreading through the economy.
The Bank of England holds its main rate at 3.75% and aims for 2% inflation. Traders widely expect it to raise rates on 5 November, which would be its first increase since 2023. Some market pricing points to at least three rises by April 2027.
The government's forecasts in the Budget show inflation peaking at 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027.
levels.why: Rate decisions affect mortgages, savings and the cost of borrowing for firms.

levels.headline: Inflation hits 3.5%, raising hopes the Bank of England will lift rates
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier. That is up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% that experts predicted. Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose to 2.8%.
The biggest cause was fuel. Petrol and diesel prices were 29.8% higher than a year before. Prices for services such as travel and hospitality have also risen faster, which suggests higher energy costs are spreading.
The Bank of England's main interest rate is 3.75%, and its target for inflation is 2%. Markets strongly expect it to raise rates on 5 November, the first rise since 2023. Government forecasts say inflation will peak at 3.8% in early 2027.
levels.why: Higher interest rates could make mortgages and loans more expensive.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5%, and an interest rate rise is expected
levels.body:
Inflation in the UK, the rate prices rise, went up to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August. Experts had expected 3.4%. A measure that leaves out food and energy, called core inflation, rose to 2.8%.
Fuel was the main reason. Petrol and diesel cost 29.8% more than a year ago. Prices for services have also risen faster, which shows that high energy costs are spreading through the economy.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate, now 3.75%. Its target for inflation is 2%. Investors strongly expect it to raise the rate on 5 November, which would be its first rise since 2023. Government forecasts say inflation will peak at 3.8% early in 2027.
levels.why: A rate rise would affect people with mortgages and loans.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, so interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Inflation means prices rising over time. In September, UK prices were 3.5% higher than a year before. In August the figure was 3.1%. Experts had thought it would be 3.4%.
Petrol and diesel are the biggest reason. They cost nearly 30% more than a year ago. Prices for services, like travel and eating out, have also gone up faster.
The Bank of England is in charge of the main interest rate. That rate is 3.75% now. It wants inflation to be 2%. Many experts think the Bank will raise the rate on 5 November, for the first time since 2023. Raising rates is a way to slow price rises.
The government thinks inflation will peak at 3.8% early in 2027.
levels.why: Higher rates make borrowing cost more but can help keep prices steady.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster and the Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates

levels.headline: Prices rose faster in September, so interest rates may go up

Inflation is how fast prices go up. In September, UK prices were 3.5% higher than a year earlier. In August the figure was 3.1%. That is quicker than experts expected.

levels.why: Interest rates change what families pay on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Why prices are rising and interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Inflation means things cost more than before. In September, prices in the UK were 3.5% higher than a year ago. A pound buys a bit less than it did.
The biggest cause is fuel. Petrol and diesel cost almost 30% more than a year ago. Other things, like travel, are getting dearer too.
There is a special bank for the whole country, the Bank of England. It sets an interest rate. This is the extra price you pay to borrow money, or the reward you get for saving. The rate is 3.75% now. Many people think the Bank will raise it on 5 November. It does this to slow down price rises.
The government thinks prices will rise fastest in early 2027.
levels.why: It affects the cost of borrowing and what your money can buy.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, and borrowing may cost more
levels.body:
Prices go up over time. This is called inflation. In September, things in the UK cost 3.5% more than a year before. A pound buys a little less than it did.
Petrol and diesel are a big reason. They cost almost 30% more than last year. Other things like travel cost more too.
The Bank of England is like the country's money manager. It sets an interest rate, which is the price of borrowing money. If you borrow, you pay extra. If you save, you get extra. The rate is 3.75% now. Many people think the Bank will raise it on 5 November to slow price rises.
The government thinks prices will rise fastest early next year.
levels.why: A higher rate can make loans cost more but can help prices calm down.

levels.headline: Prices go up, and so might the cost of borrowing
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet that cost £1 last year. Now it costs a bit more. When lots of things cost more, that is called inflation. In September, prices in the UK were 3.5% higher than last year.
Petrol and diesel have gone up the most. They cost almost a third more than last year. That makes other things dearer too.
A bank called the Bank of England sets the price of borrowing money. If you borrow pocket money from a friend, you might pay back a little extra. That extra is interest. Many people think the Bank will make it a bit bigger on 5 November. That can help slow prices from going up so fast.
levels.why: It affects how far money goes and what families pay when they borrow.

headline: ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early in February 2027

terms.meaning: The interest rate the ECB pays banks for money left with it; its key policy rate.
The 20-odd EU countries that use the euro.
Holding rates while signalling that rises may follow.

levels.headline: ECB holds rates at 2.5% as Lagarde announces she will leave early in February 2027
levels.body:
The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October, after two rate rises this year, the latest in September. Inflation across the euro area has reached 3.8%, almost double the ECB's 2% target and the highest since September 2023, driven mainly by energy costs linked to the war involving Iran.
President Christine Lagarde said the decision was unanimous but that policymakers seriously debated a rise. Markets read it as a hawkish pause, with traders pricing about a 67% chance of a quarter-point increase in December.
Lagarde also said she will leave on 7 February 2027, around nine months before her eight-year term ends, saying she cannot "remain neutral" given recent developments. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as leading candidates to succeed her. The European Council will appoint the new president.
levels.why: The ECB's rate decisions shape borrowing costs across Europe, and its next leader will steer them.

levels.headline: ECB pauses at 2.5% while Lagarde confirms an early exit
levels.body:
The European Central Bank held its key interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October after raising rates twice this year, most recently in September. Euro area inflation is 3.8%, the highest since September 2023 and nearly double the 2% target, with energy costs the main driver.
Christine Lagarde said the decision to hold was unanimous, though a rise was seriously discussed. Traders see a pause with a bias to tighten, and price about a 67% chance of a rise in December.
Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027, some nine months before her term was due to end, saying she cannot "remain neutral". Pablo Hernández de Cos of Spain and Klaas Knot of the Netherlands are seen as frontrunners to replace her, and the European Council will make the choice.
levels.why: Changes at the top of the ECB could affect how Europe handles high inflation.

levels.headline: ECB holds interest rates and Lagarde says she will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank left its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It had raised rates twice this year, the last time in September. Inflation in the euro area is 3.8%, the highest since September 2023 and well above the 2% target. High energy costs are the main cause.
President Christine Lagarde said the vote to hold was unanimous but that members seriously discussed raising rates. Investors think a rise in December is likely, giving it about a 67% chance.
Lagarde also announced she will leave on 7 February 2027, about nine months before her eight-year term ends. She said she cannot "remain neutral" given recent developments. Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot are seen as likely successors.
levels.why: Interest rates in the euro area affect loans, savings and prices for millions of people.

levels.headline: European Central Bank keeps rates at 2.5% and its president says she is leaving
levels.body:
The European Central Bank (ECB) kept its main interest rate at 2.5% on 29 October. It is the bank for the countries that use the euro. It raised rates twice this year to fight rising prices. Inflation there is now 3.8%, nearly double its 2% target, mostly because energy costs are high.
The president, Christine Lagarde, said all members agreed to hold, but they talked seriously about raising rates. Investors now think there is about a 67% chance of a rise in December.
Lagarde also said she will leave on 7 February 2027, around nine months early. She said she cannot "remain neutral" when she sees what is happening. Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are seen as possible replacements.
levels.why: The ECB's choices affect prices and borrowing costs in countries that use the euro.

levels.headline: European bank leaves interest rates alone, and its boss will leave early
levels.body:
The European Central Bank, or ECB, looks after money for countries that use the euro. On 29 October it kept its main interest rate at 2.5%. It raised the rate twice earlier this year to fight rising prices, which are called inflation.
Prices in these countries are now rising by 3.8% a year. The ECB wants only 2%. The main reason is the high cost of energy. All the members agreed to keep rates the same, but they talked seriously about raising them. Investors think there is a good chance of a rise in December.
The boss, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave in February 2027, nine months before she had to. Two names being talked about to replace her are Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot.
levels.why: Interest rates change what people pay on loans and earn on savings in Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's central bank holds rates; its leader says she will step down
levels.body:
Many countries in Europe share one kind of money, the euro. One bank, the European Central Bank, sets the main interest rate for them. On 29 October it kept that rate at 2.5%. It had raised it twice this year.
Prices in these countries are rising by 3.8% a year. That is almost twice what the bank wants, which is 2%. Energy costs are the main reason. People who watch the bank think it might raise the rate in December.
The boss of the bank, Christine Lagarde, also said she will leave in February 2027. That is about nine months earlier than planned. People have named two possible new bosses, Pablo Hernández de Cos from Spain and Klaas Knot from the Netherlands.
levels.why: It affects prices, loans and savings for many people in Europe.

levels.headline: Europe's money bank pauses and its boss will leave
levels.body:
Lots of countries in Europe use the same money, called the euro. A bank called the European Central Bank looks after it. On 29 October, this bank said it would not change its main interest rate. It stays at 2.5%.
Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or get when you save. The bank had put the rate up twice this year, because prices were rising too fast. Prices there are going up by 3.8% a year. The bank wants only 2%. High energy costs are the main cause.
The boss, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave in February 2027. That is early. People are talking about who might replace her.
levels.why: It helps decide how much it costs to borrow money in Europe.

levels.headline: A big bank keeps its rate the same
levels.body:
A group of countries in Europe all use the same money, the euro. They share one big bank that looks after it. It is called the European Central Bank.
On 29 October, the bank said it would keep its interest rate at 2.5%. Interest is the extra you pay when you borrow money. Prices have been going up fast, partly because energy costs a lot. The bank had raised the rate twice this year to help slow this down. It may raise it again in December.
The boss of the bank, Christine Lagarde, also said she will leave in February 2027. That is earlier than planned. A new boss will be picked by leaders in Europe.
levels.why: Its choices can change how much things cost for families in Europe.

levels.headline: A big bank in Europe makes a choice
levels.body:
Imagine a class where everyone uses the same pretend money. One student is the banker and decides how much extra to charge when someone borrows. In real life, a big bank does this for many countries in Europe. It is called the European Central Bank.
On 29 October, the banker said the extra charge, called the interest rate, would stay at 2.5%. Prices have been going up quickly, partly because energy costs a lot. The bank wants prices to rise slowly. It may raise the charge again in December.
The head of the bank, Christine Lagarde, said she will leave in February 2027. That is earlier than planned. Leaders will choose someone new.
levels.why: It matters because the cost of borrowing touches many families.

headline: European gas price crosses €100 for the first time since 2022 as the EU warns of a new energy crisis

levels.headline: European gas price crosses €100 for the first time since 2022 as the EU warns of a new energy crisis
levels.body:
The benchmark European gas price rose above €100 per megawatt-hour on Wednesday 28 October for the first time since the 2022 crisis. The front-month Dutch TTF contract traded at €100.37 at 16:00 CET, up more than 4%. It remains well below the record of about €340 in August 2022.
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said: "Once again, due to geopolitical turbulence, Europe faces another energy crisis." EU gas storage stood at 75% on 21 October, according to ACER, short of the usual target of 90% by 1 November, which countries have been allowed to apply more flexibly.
Jørgensen has urged governments to keep cutting gas and electricity demand. Goldman Sachs analysts had said prices would need to rise above €100 to curb Asian demand if Middle East LNG exports recover only gradually through 2027.
levels.why: Gas prices feed into household bills, industry costs and inflation across Europe.

levels.headline: European gas tops €100 for the first time since 2022
levels.body:
European wholesale gas prices rose above €100 per megawatt-hour on 28 October for the first time since 2022. The Dutch TTF benchmark hit €100.37 at 16:00 CET, up more than 4% on the day. The record is about €340, set in August 2022.
The EU's Energy Commissioner, Dan Jørgensen, warned that "Europe faces another energy crisis" because of geopolitical turbulence. According to ACER, EU gas storage was 75% full on 21 October, below the usual 90% target for 1 November, though countries have been given flexibility.
Jørgensen has asked governments to keep reducing gas and electricity use. Goldman Sachs analysts have said prices above €100 could be needed to curb Asian demand if Middle East liquefied gas exports recover slowly through 2027.
levels.why: Higher wholesale gas prices usually mean higher energy bills and inflation later.

levels.headline: Gas prices in Europe pass €100 as the EU warns of a new crisis
levels.body:
Gas prices in Europe went above €100 per megawatt-hour on 28 October. This is the first time since 2022. The Dutch TTF price, the main European benchmark, reached €100.37, up more than 4% in a day. It is still far below the record of about €340 in August 2022.
EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said Europe "faces another energy crisis". Gas stores in the EU were 75% full on 21 October, short of the normal 90% target for 1 November, although countries can be flexible about it.
Jørgensen wants governments to keep cutting how much gas and electricity people use. Goldman Sachs analysts said prices might need to go above €100 to reduce demand in Asia if Middle East gas exports return only slowly.
levels.why: It can push up bills and prices for households and businesses.

levels.headline: Gas prices jump in Europe

Gas is used to heat homes and to make electricity. In Europe, gas got very expensive. The price went above €100 for a standard amount, which has not happened since 2022.

levels.headline: Keeping warm gets pricey

Many homes in Europe use gas to stay warm and to cook. Gas has become very expensive. The price went above €100 for a standard amount, the first time since 2022.

headline: Spain train crash death toll revised to 69 as investigators examine a 'inexplicable' control centre order

terms.meaning: A recorder in a train that stores data to help investigators work out what happened.

levels.headline: Spain train crash death toll revised to 69 as investigators examine a 'inexplicable' control centre order
levels.body:
The death toll from Wednesday's high-speed train collision near Urda in Toledo province, on the Madrid to Seville line, has been revised to 69 from the 74 first reported by the transport ministry. Spain's Railway Accident Investigation Commission gave the lower figure, and about 50 people were reported injured.
A Renfe high-speed train struck the rear of a stopped Iryo service. A safety system failed on the stretch of track, halting several trains. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called a control centre order to resume normal running "inexplicable" and said the drivers were not to blame.
A court in Orgaz has ordered the trains' black boxes seized and a two-kilometre zone around the site closed. Investigators will seek records from the Adif control centre in Madrid. It is Spain's second deadly high-speed collision this year, after the January crash in Adamuz, Córdoba.
levels.why: The crash raises serious questions about rail safety in a country that relies heavily on high-speed trains.

levels.headline: Spain train crash toll revised to 69 as control centre order is investigated

levels.headline: Spain train crash: 69 dead as investigators look at a control centre order

At least 69 people died when two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in Toledo province, on the Madrid to Seville line. Officials lowered the toll from 74 after checking the figures. About 50 people were injured.

levels.headline: A very sad accident on a train track

In Spain, there was a very sad accident. Two fast trains crashed. Many people died and others were hurt. Their families and friends are very sad.

Now special helpers called investigators are working hard. They are looking at the trains' black boxes, which are like a diary of what the trains did. They want to find out why it happened so it will not happen again.

headline: Israel faces weeks of coalition talks as neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's reaches 61 seats

terms.meaning: A government formed by several parties that agree to work together.
Israel's parliament, with 120 seats.
A group whose support decides who can govern.

levels.headline: Israel faces weeks of coalition talks as neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's reaches 61 seats
levels.body:
Israel's election has left neither side with a governing majority. According to the Central Elections Committee, Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its hard-right allies won 53 seats, down from 64 in 2022. The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48. The Joint List and Ra'am won a combined 19, a record for Arab-led parties. A majority needs 61 of the 120 seats.
Turnout was around 77.7%, the highest in 27 years. President Isaac Herzog will consult parties and name the person best placed to form a government. A coalition has 28 days to form, extendable by up to 14, otherwise new elections follow, with Netanyahu staying in office meanwhile.
Likud alleges Arab-led parties "stole" the election, without evidence. The Shin Bet has been asked to investigate suspicions of improper foreign funding, which Qatar denies. Results are due to be certified by 4 November, and the new Knesset is sworn in on 10 November.
levels.why: The result decides who leads Israel during the Gaza and Iran conflicts and could force another election.

levels.headline: Israel's election leaves Netanyahu and Eisenkot short of a majority
levels.body:
Israel's final count shows no clear winner. Netanyahu's Likud and its hard-right allies won 53 seats, against 64 in 2022. Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc won 48, and Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra'am, won 19 together, an all-time high. A governing majority needs 61 of 120 seats.
Turnout was around 77.7%, the highest for 27 years. President Herzog will consult the parties and pick someone to try to build a coalition, which has 28 days, extendable by up to 14. If it fails, new elections are called, and Netanyahu stays in office meanwhile.
Likud claims Arab-led parties "stole" the election, offering no evidence. The Shin Bet has been asked to examine suspected foreign funding, which Qatar denies. Results should be certified by 4 November.
levels.why: Coalition talks will shape Israel's policy on war, security and the economy.

levels.headline: No clear winner in Israel's election as both blocs miss a majority
levels.body:
Israel's election has produced no clear winner. Netanyahu's Likud and its hard-right allies won 53 seats, down from 64 in 2022. The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48. Arab-led parties won 19 between them, their best ever. To govern, a bloc needs 61 of the 120 seats in parliament.
Around 77.7% of voters turned out, the highest for 27 years. President Herzog will ask a party leader to try to form a government, with 28 days to do it, plus up to 14 more. If that fails, there will be another election, and Netanyahu stays in office in the meantime.
Likud says Arab-led parties "stole" the vote but has given no evidence. The Shin Bet has been asked to investigate suspected foreign funding, which Qatar denies.
levels.why: A deadlock could leave Israel without a stable government at a tense time.

levels.headline: Israel's vote ends without a winner, and weeks of talks begin
levels.body:
Israel's election has not produced a clear winner. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party, Likud, and its hard-right allies won 53 seats. That is down from 64 at the last election in 2022. levels.why: The outcome decides who leads Israel and whether voters must go back to the polls.

levels.headline: Israel's election leaves nobody with enough seats to govern
levels.body:
Israel held an election, but nobody won enough seats to govern alone. The parliament, called the Knesset, has 120 seats. A group needs 61 to have a majority. Benjamin Netanyahu's party, Likud, and its allies won 53. Gadi Eisenkot's group won 48. Arab-led parties won 19, the most they have ever won.

Likud says the election was "stolen", but has not given evidence.
levels.why: Without a stable government, big decisions on war and the economy could be delayed.

levels.headline: Israel's election has no clear winner
levels.body:
Israel has just had an election, but nobody won enough seats to run the country. The parliament has 120 seats, and a group needs 61 to have a majority. Benjamin Netanyahu's party and its allies won 53. Gadi Eisenkot's group won 48. Arab-led parties won 19, which is more than ever before.

levels.why: It decides who leads Israel next and whether there will be another vote.

levels.headline: Israel votes, but no one wins enough seats
levels.body:
Israel held an election. The parliament there has 120 seats. To lead, a group needs more than half, which is 61. But no group got that many.
Benjamin Netanyahu's party and its friends won 53 seats. Another group, led by Gadi Eisenkot, won 48. Parties led by Arab citizens won 19, the most they have ever won. Lots of people voted, more than in 27 years.
Now the leaders must try to team up. A team of parties that govern together is called a coalition. They have about four weeks to try. If they cannot team up, everyone will have to vote again.
Netanyahu's party says the vote was unfair, but it has not shown proof.
levels.why: It decides who runs the country and whether another vote is needed.

levels.headline: An election where nobody wins enough
levels.body:
Israel held an election to choose who will run the country. In the parliament there are 120 seats. A group needs 61 to be in charge. This time nobody got enough.
One group, led by Benjamin Netanyahu, won 53 seats. Another group, led by Gadi Eisenkot, won 48. A third set of parties won 19. Many people voted this time, more than for a very long time.
Now the groups have to talk. They need to find others to join them to make a bigger team. They have about four weeks. If they cannot, people must vote again.
One group says the vote was unfair. It has not shown any proof.
levels.why: Until a team is found, nobody is sure who will lead.

levels.headline: What happens when nobody wins enough votes
levels.body:
Imagine your class votes for a captain. You need more than half the votes to win. But two children get nearly the same, and nobody gets more than half. What happens next?
Something like this happened in Israel. The country voted for a parliament with 120 seats. A group needs 61 to be in charge. One group got 53, another got 48, and a third got 19.
Now they must talk and make teams. A team of parties is called a coalition. They have about four weeks to try. If nobody can make a team, everyone votes again.
One group says the vote was unfair, but it has not shown any proof.
levels.why: It shows why talking and agreeing matters when no one wins outright.

headline: Oil stays near $115 a barrel as peace hopes offset a reported Houthi attack on a Saudi refinery

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.

levels.headline: Oil stays near $115 a barrel as peace hopes offset a reported Houthi attack on a Saudi refinery
levels.body:
Brent crude futures fell 44 cents to settle at $114.88 a barrel on Thursday 29 October, while US West Texas Intermediate lost 78 cents to settle at $102, according to CNBC. Brent had closed at $116.72 earlier in the week, its highest settlement since 29 April.
Prices have been driven by the conflict with Iran and attacks on Saudi energy sites. Iran-allied Houthi militants said they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery with a ballistic missile. Traders are also watching whether the US might take military action against Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
On the other side, Vice President JD Vance has reportedly contacted Iran's Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, to try to restart peace talks. Meanwhile the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve held 282.6 million barrels last week, its lowest since 1982.
levels.why: High oil prices feed straight into petrol, transport and food costs and raise inflation.

levels.headline: Oil eases to about $115 as peace efforts compete with fears over Saudi attacks

Brent crude futures slipped 44 cents to settle at $114.88 a barrel on Thursday 29 October. US West Texas Intermediate fell 78 cents to $102. Earlier in the week Brent settled at $116.72, its highest close since 29 April.

Prices dipped on reports that Vice President JD Vance has contacted Iran's Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, to restart peace talks. The US emergency oil stockpile stood at 282.6 million barrels, the lowest since 1982.
levels.why: Oil costs affect fuel prices and inflation in almost every country.

levels.headline: Oil prices dip but stay high as Middle East tensions continue
levels.body:
Oil prices fell slightly on Thursday 29 October but stayed high. Brent crude, the international benchmark, closed 44 cents lower at $114.88 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate closed 78 cents lower at $102. Earlier in the week Brent reached $116.72, its highest close since 29 April.
The conflict with Iran and attacks on Saudi oil sites are keeping prices up. Houthi militants allied with Iran said they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery with a missile. Traders are also watching for possible US military action against Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
Hopes rose a little after reports that Vice President JD Vance reached out to an Iranian official to restart peace talks. America's emergency oil stockpile is at its lowest since 1982.
levels.why: Higher oil prices push up petrol costs and prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil prices ease slightly but remain near $115 a barrel
levels.body:
Oil prices dipped a little on Thursday 29 October but are still very high. Brent crude, the main international price, fell 44 cents to $114.88 a barrel. The US price, West Texas Intermediate, fell 78 cents to $102. Earlier this week Brent closed at $116.72, its highest close since 29 April.

levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol, transport and food usually cost more.

levels.headline: Oil stays very expensive as the Middle East stays tense
levels.body:
Oil is a liquid fuel used to make petrol, diesel and plastics. Its price is counted per barrel. On Thursday 29 October, a barrel of Brent crude, the main world price, cost $114.88. That is a tiny bit less than the day before. The US price was $102.

levels.headline: Oil costs a lot because of trouble in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil is used to make petrol and diesel. It is sold by the barrel. On Thursday 29 October, one barrel of Brent crude, the main world price, cost $114.88. That is slightly lower than the day before but still very high. The American price was $102.
The reason is trouble in the Middle East. There is a conflict involving Iran. A group allied with Iran said it hit a Saudi Arabian oil factory, called a refinery, with a missile. Some traders also worry America may attack Iran after its elections on 3 November.
There is a bit of hope, as one American leader has reportedly tried to restart peace talks. America's emergency oil store is at its lowest since 1982.
levels.why: Oil prices change how much petrol and many other things cost.

levels.headline: Oil is still very expensive
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. People turn it into petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. It is sold by the barrel. Today a barrel costs about $115. A few years ago, it cost much less.
Oil is dear because of trouble in the Middle East, where much of it comes from. Some fighters said they hit a big oil factory in Saudi Arabia with a missile. Also, people worry about what America might do about Iran after its elections.
There is a little hope. A leader in America reportedly asked to talk with someone in Iran about peace. America also keeps a store of oil for emergencies, and it is the lowest since 1982.
levels.why: It changes how much it costs to drive, deliver goods and buy things.

levels.headline: Why petrol and many things may cost more
levels.body:
Oil is a thick black liquid found under the ground. People use it to make petrol for cars. It is sold in big barrels, and its price goes up and down.
Right now, it costs about $115 for one barrel. That is a lot. It costs more because there is trouble in the Middle East, where much oil is made. Some fighters said they hit a big oil factory in Saudi Arabia.
When oil is dear, petrol is dear, and so are things that are driven to the shops. A leader in America has reportedly tried to speak to Iran about peace. That could help prices to come down.
levels.why: It is one reason why prices in shops and at petrol stations stay high.

levels.headline: Why fuel costs so much
levels.body:
Cars and lorries need fuel to move. Much fuel is made from oil, which comes from under the ground. It is sold in big barrels.
A barrel costs about $115 now. That is a lot of money. Think of a toy that is hard to get, so the shop charges more. Oil is hard to get when there is trouble where it is made, in the Middle East.
Some fighters said they hit an oil factory in Saudi Arabia. People are also afraid of more fighting soon.
When oil costs more, it costs more to drive things to the shops. Then the things in the shops can cost more too. Some leaders are trying to talk about peace. That could help.
levels.why: It can make the things families buy cost more.
